verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.19 (same number in the Sastri/Shankara, Govindacharya/Ramanuja, Vireswarananda/Sridhara and Sivananda editions; chapters 5-12 number identically across standard editions)
translation_note: Acceptable. 'Sarga' is literally 'creation'; Shankara glosses it as birth (janma) and Ramanuja and Sridhara as samsara, so 'the world is conquered' is looser than 'birth/the round of becoming is overcome'. our_note already follows Shankara. Note the verse continues 5.18, whose examples (learned brahmin, cow, elephant, dog, dog-eater) carry caste language.
context: Krishna has just said (5.18) that the wise look with the same eye on a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste. This verse says such people have already overcome birth and becoming while still alive, because their minds rest in Brahman, which is the same in all. It leads into 5.20's portrait of the person who is neither elated nor crushed.

key_terms.sense: birth, the round of becoming, is mastered
Brahman is flawless and the same in everything

core_teaching: A mind that rests in the sameness of the one reality in every being is already free in this life; that sameness is Brahman itself, so such people already stand in Brahman.

commentaries.gist: Even while living, sages who see the one Brahman equally in all creatures have mastered birth. Brahman only appears stained in 'impure' bodies; it is untouched. Rules about honouring people unequally apply only to those who identify with the body.

'Here' means even during practice: whoever sees all selves as equal has overcome samsara. Freed of matter's taint, the self is the same in all, so resting in that sameness is resting in Brahman; such people are as liberated.

Answers the objection that Gautama's law forbids treating unequal people alike: these sages have overcome samsara while alive and reached Brahman; the fault Gautama names applies to someone still acting as an honour-giver, before that attainment.

When the mind stays balanced, birth and death are conquered and freedom is gained. Brahman is pure and attributeless, so dwelling in an outcaste or a dog does not affect it; it is one and equal in all.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that peace is not postponed to an afterlife: a mind that stops ranking people and outcomes as higher and lower is already free of much of its torment, today.
misreadings: Not a claim that social inequality or mistreatment doesn't matter; the 'sameness' is about the one Self in all, not about ignoring injustice.
Not indifference or emotional flatness; it is steadiness of the mind.
cautions: The surrounding verse (5.18) and Shankara's discussion use caste examples ('dog-eater', rules for honouring brahmins); keep that out of a modern reading or handle it explicitly.
'Conquering birth' presupposes rebirth doctrine.

not_for: someone currently facing discrimination, who may hear 'see everyone as the same' as dismissing their experience

knower of Brahman, abiding in Brahman

translation_note: Accurate; 'wombs of sorrow' renders duḥkha-yonayaḥ literally ('sources of sorrow' is plainer).
context: Krishna has said (5.21) that one unattached to outer contacts finds happiness in the self. Here he explains why: pleasures born of contact breed sorrow and do not last. The next verse (5.23) praises the person who can withstand the surge of desire and anger before the body falls.

key_terms.sense: enjoyments born of the senses touching their objects
having a beginning and an end
the wise one does not take delight in them

core_teaching: Pleasures that depend on contact with objects start, end and leave pain behind, so a discerning person does not rest their happiness on them.

commentaries.gist: Contact-born pleasures breed sorrow, here and hereafter, being products of ignorance. They start with sense contact and end with separation, so are momentary; the discerning do not revel in them, and only the ignorant do.
Pleasures from sense contact end in sorrow and are seen to last only a short time; one who knows their real nature does not delight in them.

Answering how giving up pleasant things can be a human good: even while they last, such pleasures are mixed with rivalry and envy, so they cause sorrow; and they begin and end, so the discerning do not delight in them.
People seek joy in perishable objects and end up carrying sorrow; between the start and end is only a brief, hollow pleasure. Withdraw the senses and fix the mind on the blissful Self within.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the comedown after a purchase, a binge or a scroll: enjoy what comes, but don't stake your lasting happiness on things that, by their nature, end.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of joy, food, friendship or beauty; the point is where lasting happiness can be found.
Not a reason for guilt about ordinary pleasures.
cautions: Shankara's language is severe (he says the deeply deluded, 'like animals', delight in objects); avoid carrying that tone to a reader.
For someone with depression or anhedonia, 'pleasures breed sorrow' may reinforce hopelessness.

someone noticing a habit that no longer satisfies
a person rethinking what they've built their happiness on
not_for: someone depressed whose small pleasures are a lifeline right now

with freedom as the highest aim
from whom desire, fear and anger have gone

practical_reading: Teachers use the trio of desire, fear and anger as a check-in: notice which of the three is driving you right now, and return to the breath before acting.

cautions: For someone in real danger, 'be free of fear' should not be read as 'ignore the threat'.

translation_note: Accurate. Commentators read 'yukta' as 'established in yoga' (Sridhara: yogārūḍha); our 'steadfast' is fine.
context: Part of Krishna's portrait of the one who has climbed to yoga (yogārūḍha), after 6.7's calm in honour and insult. This verse adds inner contentment through knowledge and direct experience, and an even regard for a clod, a stone and gold. 6.9 extends the evenness to people.

key_terms.sense: content through knowledge and its realisation
to whom a clod, a stone and gold are the same

core_teaching: Someone who has both understood and directly experienced the truth is inwardly satisfied, unshaken and master of the senses, so objects that others value differently no longer pull them.

commentaries.gist: Jñāna is understanding what scripture teaches; vijñāna is making it one's own experience. Satisfied by both, the person is unshakable and sense-controlled, and is called 'joined in yoga'; earth, stone and gold are alike to him.

Content in knowing the self and its distinctness from matter; firm in the self unchanged through every body; since material things no longer please him, clod, stone and gold are equal. Such a karma-yogi is fit for meditation.

Jñāna is knowledge from teaching, vijñāna direct experience; content with these and wanting nothing, changeless and sense-controlled, he sees nothing among earth, stone and gold as to be grasped or rejected. He has climbed to yoga.

Jñāna is theoretical knowledge from study, vijñāna direct realisation. Kūṭastha means changeless like an anvil: iron is hammered on it, but it stays the same, as the yogi stays unaffected by contact with objects.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to distinguish book knowledge from lived understanding, and to describe freedom from the pull of possessions and money.
misreadings: Not a reason to neglect money, savings or family finances (our existing misuse note is right); it is about not being ruled by them.
Not anti-intellectual: knowledge is half of what satisfies the yogi.

a learner frustrated that knowing something isn't the same as living it
someone seeking contentment

key_terms.sense: well-wisher who helps without expecting return
the neutral and the impartial mediator
one who is hateful or disagreeable to us

One whose judgement toward all these, from natural well-wisher to wrongdoer, is free of attachment and aversion is superior even to the one just described.

cautions: A reader hurt by a relative or partner may hear 'be the same toward the hateful' as pressure to reconcile or forgive before they're ready.

key_terms.sense: nor for one who does not eat at all

translation_note: Accurate. Shankara specifies the worshipper as kāmī, one who worships for wished-for results; the neighbouring verses (7.20, 7.23) frame such worship as desire-driven and its fruits as limited, which our_note correctly records.
context: Krishna has said that people whose understanding is carried away by desires turn to other deities (7.20). Here he says that whatever form a devotee worships with faith, he himself makes that faith firm; 7.22 says the devotee gains his wishes, though they are granted by Krishna, and 7.23 says such results are finite, while his own devotees reach him.

key_terms.sense: whichever devotee, whichever form (of a deity)

core_teaching: God honours and steadies sincere faith in whatever form a person worships, because every such form is ultimately God's; but the context also says worship for limited ends brings limited results.

commentaries.gist: Whatever deity-form a person moved by desires wishes to worship with faith, the Lord makes that very faith steady.

Those deities are the Lord's own bodies, as the Upanishad's inner-controller passage teaches. Even when the worshipper of Indra and others does not know this, the Lord recognises the faith as aimed at his body and makes it unobstructed.
Whichever deity-form, which is really the Lord's own form, a devotee wants to worship with faith, the Lord as inner controller makes that faith firm.
Tanu means a deity here. The Lord, the indweller of all, steadies the faith of one who worships lesser divinities, a faith born of impressions from a past birth.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage respect for other people's ways of worship: sincere faith is honoured, and growth comes by deepening it, not by being mocked out of it.
misreadings: Not a simple statement that all worship is equal; 7.20 and 7.23 rank desire-driven worship below devotion to the Supreme.
Not permission to belittle someone's chosen deity or practice.
cautions: Reading it as pure pluralism skips the hierarchy in 7.20-23; reading it as sectarian skips 'I make that faith steady'. Present both.
speaks_to: interfaith families and friendships
someone unsure whether their way of worship 'counts'
a person whose faith feels unsteady
not_for: a reader looking for a proof-text that their tradition alone is right

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 7.27 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Sarge' is 'at creation / at birth'; commentators read it as at the time of birth.
context: Krishna has said he knows all beings past, present and future, but no one knows him (7.26). This verse gives the reason: from birth, the delusion of the opposites, born of desire and aversion, confuses every being. 7.28 adds that people whose wrongdoing has ended, freed from that delusion, worship him with firm resolve.

key_terms.sense: by the delusion of the pairs of opposites

core_teaching: Every being is confused from birth by the pull of wanting and the push of aversion, which split experience into pleasant and unpleasant and hide the deeper reality.

commentaries.gist: Desire and aversion, opposed like heat and cold and tied to pleasure, pain and their causes, give rise to the delusion of opposites, which overwhelms all beings at birth.
Likes and dislikes practised toward pleasure and pain in earlier births leave impressions; so at birth itself the same pairs appear as things to want or hate and delude beings.

At birth, desire for the pleasing and aversion to the unpleasant breed loss of discernment amid heat and cold, pleasure and pain; beings identify with the body ('I am happy, I am miserable'), and so do not know the Lord.
Pleasure brings attachment and pain brings aversion, rooted in the instinct to preserve the body. Overwhelmed by these, a person cannot see even the outer world as it is, let alone the inner Self.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to reactivity: much of our confusion comes from automatic liking and disliking, so noticing the pull and push is the first step toward clear sight.
misreadings: Not a claim that having preferences is sinful.
Not fatalism about human nature; 7.28 describes people freed from this delusion.
speaks_to: someone caught in reactive likes and dislikes
a person trying to understand why they keep misjudging situations
meditators working with craving and aversion
not_for: someone in crisis who needs comfort rather than a diagnosis of human confusion

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 8.6 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Translation is accurate. The line ('Whatever you keep thinking about shapes who you become, right to the end') turns a teaching about the moment of death and the next state into a general statement about thought shaping character. That is a fair application, but the verse is about death; label it as an extension.
context: Arjuna has asked, among seven questions, how the Lord is to be known at the time of death (8.2). Krishna answers that whoever leaves the body remembering him attains him (8.5), and generalises here: whatever one remembers at the end, one goes to, because one has always dwelt on it. 8.7 draws the conclusion: so remember me at all times, and fight.

key_terms.sense: leaves the body at the end
always steeped in / shaped by that state

core_teaching: What fills the mind at death determines where one goes next, and what fills the mind then is whatever one has dwelt on throughout life.

commentaries.gist: Whatever being, such as a particular deity, one thinks of when life departs, one reaches that alone, because one has practised dwelling on it; the final thought is what leads to the next body.
One reaches after death whatever one remembers at the end; and the final thought arises only about what was dwelt on earlier.

The rule is not only that remembering the Lord leads to him: whatever deity or other thing one remembers at the end, one attains; the reason is that the mind has been coloured by constant dwelling on it.

The last thought decides the next birth, and the predominant thought of a life is what occupies the mind at death; impressions from practice produce that memory. He cites the wasp and caterpillar image.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that the habits of attention we build every day are what will be left in us at the end; what we keep returning to, we become.
misreadings: Not a test that one last moment can pass or fail; every commentator ties the last thought to lifelong habit.
Not a claim that someone who died afraid, confused or unconscious is condemned.
cautions: About death and rebirth; for a bereaved reader it can trigger worry about a loved one's final moments (sudden death, dementia, sedation). Sridhara (on 8.7) notes the dying cannot make effort, which is why lifelong remembrance matters; never imply a loved one 'failed' at the end.
Not for anyone in suicidal crisis or facing imminent death without careful framing.
speaks_to: someone reflecting on what they let fill their mind
people in midlife re-examining priorities
someone preparing calmly for mortality, or caring for a dying person with faith
not_for: fresh grief, especially after a sudden or difficult death
someone with health anxiety or fear of death

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 8.7 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Accurate. The line renders 'fight' as 'keep doing your work', which matches the commentators (Shankara: do your own duty; Sivananda: 'fight' stands for one's duties).
context: Having said that the mind's final content decides one's destination (8.6), Krishna draws the conclusion for Arjuna: remember me at all times, and fight. With mind and understanding offered to him, Arjuna will surely reach him. The following verses (8.8-10) describe meditation on the supreme Person through practice.

key_terms.sense: with mind and intellect offered to me

core_teaching: Remembering God is not a retreat from life: keep God in mind all the time and keep doing your work, and with mind and judgement offered to God you will reach God.

commentaries.gist: Therefore remember the Lord at all times as scripture teaches, and fight, that is, do your own duty. With mind and intellect offered to Vasudeva you will reach him as remembered; there is no doubt.
Practise remembering me daily until death, and do your enjoined duties, including this battle. With mind and intellect offered to me, remembering me at the end, you will surely reach me.

Since only prior impressions produce memory at death, when a helpless person cannot make an effort to remember, remember me always. Constant remembrance needs a pure mind, so do your duty of fighting to purify it.
Dedicate the whole mind and intellect to the Lord and work that way. 'Fight' is suggestive: perform the duties of your station in life, which purify the heart and lead to knowledge.

practical_reading: Teachers present it as integration: carry a quiet remembrance of the divine through the workday instead of separating spiritual life from ordinary duties.
misreadings: 'Fight' means do your rightful work; it is not a call to pick battles or endorse violence (our existing misuse note is right).
Not a claim that remembering God guarantees worldly success.
cautions: Ramanuja and Sivananda frame duty in caste-and-stage-of-life terms; a modern reading should speak of one's responsibilities, not caste duty.
speaks_to: someone who feels their busy life leaves no room for spirituality
a person wanting to work with a calmer, offered mind
someone torn between duty and devotion
not_for: someone in a conflict where 'fight' could be heard literally
a reader facing death who needs comfort rather than an instruction

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 8.8 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Translation is accurate. The line ('you reach what you meditate on') generalises: the verse says one reaches the supreme divine Person by meditating on him. Setting ('steady remembrance and the cycles of creation') is fine for the passage, but cycles of creation come only in 8.16-19.
context: After 'remember me at all times and fight' (8.7), Krishna explains how remembrance becomes steady: a mind trained by repeated practice, not straying elsewhere, reaches the supreme divine Person. 8.9-10 then describe that Person and the yogi's meditation at the hour of death.

key_terms.sense: joined to the discipline of repeated practice
with a mind that does not wander to anything else

core_teaching: Steady remembrance is built by practice: repeatedly bringing the mind back to one object until it stops wandering is the means of reaching the Supreme.

commentaries.gist: Practice is repeating one thought of the Lord, uninterrupted by any other; that is yoga. With the mind so occupied, meditating as scripture and teacher instruct, one reaches the supreme Person, the one in the sun's orb.

Practice means training the mind on the object of meditation even at times outside set worship and duties. Thinking of the Lord at death with a mind so trained, one reaches him, gaining glory comparable to his.
Practice, a stream of like thoughts, is the inner means of continuous remembrance; with that one-pointed, non-wandering mind, meditating on the luminous supreme Lord, one reaches him.

Abhyasa is constant repetition of one idea of God, shutting out other thoughts and keeping a continuous flow of the divine thought; like rivers losing their names in the ocean, the sage becomes one with the Supreme.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to any devotional or meditative habit: the mind is trained not by one great effort but by returning, again and again, to the same point.
misreadings: Not a technique to get whatever you visualise; the object is the Supreme.
Not a demand that the mind never wander; practice is the returning.
speaks_to: someone building a daily prayer or meditation habit
a distracted mind that keeps drifting
someone wondering how 'remembering God always' is possible
not_for: someone who feels guilty for a wandering mind and may hear 'not straying' as a standard they fail

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 8.14 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Accurate. Data: prasang is null; the verse sits in the 8.5-16 passage on remembrance at death and the goal of no return.
context: Krishna has just described the yogi who leaves the body uttering Om and remembering him (8.12-13). Here he offers an easier assurance: for the one who remembers him constantly, every day, with mind on nothing else, he is easy to reach. 8.15-16 add that great souls who reach him do not return to rebirth, the home of sorrow.

key_terms.sense: with a mind turned to nothing else
constantly, and day after day, for a long time
of one always joined in yoga

core_teaching: God is not remote or hard to reach for someone who keeps God in mind steadily over a lifetime; constancy, more than intensity, makes the difference.

commentaries.gist: 'Constantly' means without break; 'always' means over a long time, not six months or a year but for life. To the yogi whose mind goes to nothing else and who remembers the Lord thus, he is easily reached.

One who loves the Lord so much that he cannot sustain himself without remembering him: for such a one the Lord himself, unable to bear separation, chooses him, ripens his worship and removes what stands in the way.
Reaching the Lord by concentration at death comes only through daily practice. To one who remembers him every day with mind on nothing else, he is easily attained, and not to others.
Lifelong constant remembrance is the easiest way to reach the Lord. Remembering by fits and starts, a few months on and then off, does not get there.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as encouragement: a small, unbroken daily remembrance (a name, a prayer, a pause) brings the divine near more surely than occasional intense effort.
misreadings: Not a claim that God is unreachable for those who forget or lapse; the stress is on how near God is to the constant.
Not a call to give up all other thoughts and responsibilities.
cautions: Sivananda's line that on-and-off remembrance does not reach God could discourage someone restarting a practice; foreground 'easy to reach'.
speaks_to: someone who feels God is distant
a person building a simple daily practice
someone who prefers steadiness over dramatic spiritual experiences
not_for: someone in guilt over lapses in practice who may hear 'only the constant'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 9.6 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Accurate. Data: prasang is null; the verse illustrates the paradox of 9.4-5 ('all beings are in me, yet not in me').
context: Krishna has just stated a paradox: all beings rest in him, yet he is not contained in them, and in another sense they do not rest in him; behold his divine power (9.4-5). This verse gives the image: as the vast wind, moving everywhere, always stays in space, so all beings are in him. 9.7-8 go on to the cycles in which beings dissolve into and re-emerge from his nature.

key_terms.sense: the great wind that goes everywhere

core_teaching: All beings, however restless, exist within the divine the way moving wind exists within space: held and contained, yet without the divine being touched or limited by them.

commentaries.gist: As the great, all-moving wind always stays in space, so all beings stay in the Lord, all-pervading like space, without any contact.
As the mighty wind is held and moves in supportless space by the Lord's power, so all beings rest in him, unseen. He cites a verse naming clouds, tides, moon's phases and winds as Vishnu's marvels.
Shows by example a support-and-supported relation without contact: wind, though vast and everywhere, needs space yet is not attached to it, since space has no parts; so all beings rest in the Lord.

practical_reading: Teachers use the image for anxiety and restlessness: however much your life is blowing about, it is still held in a stillness that is not disturbed by it.
misreadings: Not a claim that the world is unimportant to God.
speaks_to: anxiety and a sense of constant motion
feeling unsupported or rootless
someone who wants an image of being held
not_for: someone who needs practical support rather than a metaphysical image

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 9.17 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Acceptable. 'Dhātā' is rendered 'the one who holds it up'; Shankara and Sridhara gloss it as dispenser of the fruits of action, Ramanuja as an agent of birth besides the parents, Sivananda allows 'supporter'. 'Ordainer/sustainer' would be closer to the commentaries; our_note already follows Shankara. Data: prasang is null.
context: In a run of verses (9.16-19) Krishna names himself as every part of worship and of the world: the ritual, the offering, the fire (9.16); here, father, mother, sustainer and grandfather of the world, the one to be known, the purifier, Om and the three Vedas. 9.18 continues: the goal, supporter, witness, refuge and friend.

key_terms.sense: ordainer/dispenser (of the fruits of action), sustainer
what is to be known, the purifier, the syllable Om

core_teaching: The divine relates to the world as every kind of parent and source: begetting, nurturing, sustaining, preceding it, and also as what is worth knowing and what makes pure.

commentaries.gist: The Lord is the world's father, mother, dispenser of the fruits of action and grandsire; also what is to be known, the purifier, Om, and the Rig, Sama and Yajur Vedas.
The Lord himself stands to this universe of moving and unmoving things as father, mother, patriarch and grandsire; he is also the one to be known, the holy, Om, and the three Vedas.
Dhātā is the dispenser of the fruits of action; the purifier is what cleanses, such as expiation; Om and the Vedas too are the Lord.

Dhātā can mean supporter or dispenser of fruits. He maps father to the Lord with attributes, mother to primordial Nature, grandfather to the absolute Brahman; the purifier is like a bath in the Ganga or Gayatri japa.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to widen the image of God beyond one role: the same presence that begets also mothers, sustains and purifies, which can comfort people who feel unparented.
misreadings: Not a replacement for a parent who is gone (our existing misuse note is right).
Not a gendered claim that God is only male; the verse names God as mother as well.
cautions: Parent imagery can hurt readers with absent, abusive or recently deceased parents; use gently.
speaks_to: someone who feels alone or unparented
new parents reflecting on what parenting means
someone who wants a warmer, more familial image of God
not_for: someone whose parent was abusive, unless framed carefully
fresh grief for a parent, where it may feel like a substitution

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 9.34 (same in all editions checked; first half recurs as 18.65, which adds a promise; checked in Sivananda's text)
translation_note: Accurate. our_note's cross-reference to 18.65 is correct.
context: This is the closing verse of chapter 9. Krishna has said that a leaf, flower, fruit or water offered with love is accepted (9.26), that everything one does should be offered to him (9.27), and that even a wrongdoer who turns to him wholeheartedly is to be counted good (9.30). He sums up the whole path of devotion here: mind, love, worship and reverence turned to him.

key_terms.sense: let your mind be on me
with me as the supreme goal

core_teaching: Devotion engages the whole person, thought, love, action and humility, and a life gathered toward God in this way arrives at God.

commentaries.gist: Fix your mind on Vasudeva, be devoted, worship and bow to him; having concentrated the mind with him as the highest goal, you will reach him, who is the Self of all beings and their supreme goal.
Let the heart rest on the Lord unbroken, like a stream of poured oil: Lord of all, free of flaw, home of every excellence, lotus-eyed, cloud-hued, radiant; so devotion becomes loving contemplation.
Concluding the mode of worship: mind on me, be my devotee and servant, worship me, bow to me; with me as the highest aim and mind fixed, you will reach me, who am supreme bliss.
Fill your mind with the Lord and put head, heart and hands to him; surrender without reserve and life is transformed, sorrow falls away, and one crosses beyond death.

practical_reading: Teachers present it as a four-part daily practice anyone can begin with: a thought, a feeling of love, a small offering, and a bow.
misreadings: Not a demand to abandon family or work; the chapter's offering includes everything one does (9.27).
Not exclusivist hostility to others; it describes wholehearted devotion.
cautions: The verses just before (9.32-33) contain caste and gender hierarchy language; do not pull that context into a reading without addressing it.
speaks_to: someone wanting a simple, whole-hearted devotional practice
a person whose spiritual life feels scattered
someone longing for closeness to God
not_for: a reader alienated by devotional, personal-God language

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 10.1 (same in all editions checked; opens chapter 10)
translation_note: Minor. 'Prīyamāṇāya' means 'to you who are delighted (by hearing)'; Shankara (Sastri) says Arjuna delights in the words as if drinking nectar. Govindacharya's Ramanuja renders it '(My) beloved', explaining 'because you delight in hearing my greatness', so 'dear to me' has some support in Ramanuja, but the plain sense is 'you who delight'. Our line makes being dear the reason ('because you are dear to me'). Suggest: 'Listen again to my highest word. I speak it for your good, since you delight in it.' Data: the sanskrit field fuses the speaker label ('श्री भगवानुवाचभूय'); prasang is null.
context: Chapters 7 to 9 have described the Lord to be worshipped and briefly named his glories. Chapter 10 opens with Krishna offering, unasked, to speak again, because Arjuna delights in hearing and for his good. What follows is the teaching that no one knows his origin (10.2-3), the 'seed' verses of devotion (10.8-11), and then the long list of his glories.

key_terms.sense: to you who are delighted (by it)
out of wish for your good

core_teaching: The teacher speaks again, without being asked, because the student is delighted to listen and because the teacher wants the student's good.

commentaries.gist: Hear once more my supreme word, which reveals the highest reality; I speak it to you who delight in my words as if drinking nectar, out of a wish for your good.
Because you rejoice at hearing of my greatness, and wishing your good, namely the birth and growth of devotion to me, I will speak further about my glory; listen with attention.
Chapters 7 to 9 described the Lord to be worshipped and touched on his glories; chapter 10 lays them out in detail so that one can see the Lord everywhere.

practical_reading: Teachers draw from it that eagerness to learn draws out the teacher, and that the Gita's teaching is offered as care for the listener's good.
misreadings: Not a claim that only the 'dear' or chosen deserve the teaching.
speaks_to: someone who loves learning about the sacred
a reader who wants to feel the teaching is offered for their good
a student-teacher or mentor relationship
not_for: someone who needs a concrete teaching, since this verse is a preface

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 10.9 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Mad-gata-prāṇāḥ' is read by Shankara either as 'senses gathered into me' or 'lives given to me'; our 'lives given to me' follows his second option.
context: Krishna has said that the wise, knowing him as the source of all, worship him with love (10.8). Here he describes how such devotees live: minds on him, lives given to him, enlightening one another and always speaking of him, content and joyful. 10.10-11 add that he gives them the yoga of understanding and, out of compassion, lights the lamp of knowledge in their hearts.

key_terms.sense: lives (or senses) given over to me
they are content and they delight

core_teaching: Devotion flourishes in company: people who share a love of God and speak of it together find contentment and joy in that sharing.

commentaries.gist: Minds on the Lord, their senses drawn into him or their lives given to him, they teach one another and speak of him as endowed with knowledge, strength and power, and find contentment and delight as in a beloved.

Unable to sustain themselves without the Lord, they tell each other the qualities each has experienced and narrate his lovely deeds; the speakers are content in speaking for its own sake, the listeners delight beyond measure in hearing.
This is worship born of love: with minds and senses given to the Lord, the wise explain him to one another with reasoning and scripture and sing of him, and are always content and delighted.
The devotee's life is consecrated to the Lord; he delights in talking of the Lord's wisdom and power and feels the satisfaction of being in the company of the Beloved.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to satsang and spiritual friendship: speaking about what you love with others who love it deepens both understanding and joy.
misreadings: Not a call to talk only about God or to withdraw from other relationships.
speaks_to: someone missing a spiritual community
friends or couples who share a faith
a person whose devotion feels lonely
study and discussion groups
not_for: someone hurt by a religious group, for whom community talk may sting
someone isolated with no such company, unless offered as an invitation

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 10.20 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Guḍākeśa' (Arjuna) means 'conqueror of sleep' or 'thick-haired' (Shankara gives both).
context: Arjuna has asked Krishna to describe his glories in full, so that he can meditate on him in them (10.16-18). Krishna begins the list with this verse: first and foremost he is the self in the heart of every being, and the beginning, middle and end of all beings. The particular glories follow from 10.21 (among the Adityas, Vishnu; among lights, the sun...).

key_terms.sense: seated in the heart of all beings

key_terms.term: ādiś ca madhyaṃ ca ... anta eva ca
key_terms.sense: the beginning, the middle and the end

core_teaching: The divine is first of all the innermost self present in every heart, and the source, sustenance and end of every being's life.

commentaries.gist: The Lord is the inner Self in the heart of all beings, always to be meditated on; one unable to do so should meditate on him in the glories that follow. He is beings' origin, continuance and dissolution.
All beings are the Lord's body and he dwells in their hearts as their self, which means their support, controller and owner; he cites 15.15 and 18.61.
First he states his own sovereign form: as inner controller with omniscience he dwells in all minds; he is the cause of every being's birth, life and end.
Meditate on the Lord as the innermost Self. Those who can meditate on the Self as non-different are the best-prepared aspirants; others should think of him in the things listed next.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to turn the search inward: before looking for God in great things, notice the presence in your own heart and in others', through every stage of life.
misreadings: Not a claim that our impulses are God's voice; commentators speak of the self as witness and controller, not of every thought.
cautions: 'The end of beings' touches on death; mild, but notice it in grief contexts.
speaks_to: someone who feels God is far away
a person at a life transition (birth, midlife, ageing)
someone wanting to see the sacred in others
not_for: fresh grief, if 'I am the end of beings' would sound like God caused the death

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 11.24 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Accurate ('dhṛti' = steadiness/courage, 'śama' = calm).
context: Krishna has granted Arjuna divine sight to see his cosmic form (11.8). Arjuna praises the vision (11.15-22), then admits that the worlds are terrified, and so is he (11.23). In this verse he says his inner self trembles and he finds neither courage nor peace; next he sees the warriors of both armies rushing into its blazing mouths (11.25-30).
core_teaching: Faced with the full, overwhelming reality of the divine, Arjuna's courage and calm give way; the Gita lets even its hero be honestly terrified.

commentaries.gist: Glosses the vision: reaching the heavens, blazing, many frightening colours and shapes, mouths gaping, eyes huge and flaming; seeing it, Arjuna's inner self is terrified and he finds neither firmness nor peace.
'Touching the sky' means reaching the supreme heaven beyond material nature, as the Vedic texts use the word; the form is the support of matter and souls in every state.
Not only am I afraid: seeing you filling the sky, radiant, many-coloured, mouths open and great eyes blazing, my mind is shaken and I find neither steadiness nor calm.
Dhṛti can also mean patience and strength, and śama self-control; the cosmic vision has frightened Arjuna considerably.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to validate overwhelm: meeting something too vast to process (a diagnosis, a disaster, the scale of loss) can shake even a strong person, and saying so honestly is where steadiness begins.
misreadings: Not a sign that Arjuna's faith failed; terror before the infinite is a recognised religious response.
Not a picture of God as a monster; the chapter ends in the gentle form (11.49-51).
cautions: The surrounding verses (11.26-30) describe warriors crushed between teeth; avoid quoting that imagery to a frightened or grieving reader.
Pair with 11.49-51, where Krishna calms Arjuna.
speaks_to: overwhelm in the face of something vast
panic and loss of footing
awe and dread together
someone who feels they should be braver
not_for: someone in acute panic or trauma, unless paired with the reassurance of 11.49
children, given the violent imagery nearby

key_terms.sense: thinking of you as a friend

core_teaching: Seeing who his friend truly is, Arjuna regrets the casual way he treated him, and admits it came both from carelessness and from love.

context: Krishna's ladder in 12.8-11 runs from the most demanding to the most accessible: fix mind and intellect on him (12.8); if not, practise (12.9); if not, work for him (12.10); if not, give up the fruits of action (12.11). 12.12 then praises the last step. This is the third rung: if even practice is too hard, make works done for him your aim; even that leads to perfection.

key_terms.sense: if you are unable even to practise
make work for me your highest aim
even doing actions for my sake

core_teaching: When focused inner practice is too hard, action done for God's sake is itself a full path, leading step by step to perfection.

commentaries.gist: If you cannot manage practice, be devoted to works done for the Lord; even without practice, doing actions for him brings perfection, by way of a purified mind, then concentration, then knowledge.

Do the Lord's works with great love: building temples, tending gardens, lighting lamps, sweeping and cleaning, gathering flowers, worship, chanting his names, circling and bowing. Doing these soon leads to steady remembrance and to him.
If unable to practise, make central the acts done to please the Lord, such as fasting on Ekadashi, vows and singing his names; even such acts, done for him, bring liberation.

Mere actions for the Lord bring purity of mind, then meditation, knowledge and liberation. Serving humanity while feeling you serve the Lord in all is also action for his sake, together with worship and meditation.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to people who find meditation hard: serve, cook, clean, volunteer, care for others, and do it as an offering; that counts fully.
misreadings: Not 'any work is spiritual'; the point is work done for God's sake.
Not a lesser path to be ashamed of; Krishna says it reaches perfection.
speaks_to: someone who can't sit still for meditation
volunteers, carers and people whose devotion is practical
someone who feels unspiritual because they are always busy
not_for: someone already overworking, who may hear 'do more' (pair with 12.11's letting go)

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 12.11 (same number in the Sastri/Shankara, Govindacharya/Ramanuja, Vireswarananda/Sridhara and Sivananda editions)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Mad-yogam ashritah' is read differently: Shankara (Sastri) and Sivananda take it as relying on offering all actions to the Lord; Ramanuja takes 'mad-yoga' as bhakti-yoga itself; Sridhara as surrendering to the Lord alone. 'Taking refuge in my yoga' covers all three.
context: Last rung of the ladder in 12.8-11: fix the mind on Krishna; if not, practise; if not, work for his sake (12.10); and if even that is too hard, give up the fruit of all actions. The next verse (12.12) then praises this last, most accessible step, and 12.13-20 describe the person who lives it.

key_terms.sense: if you are unable to do even this
relying on union with me / on offering acts to me
giving up the fruit of all actions

core_teaching: Even someone who cannot meditate, practise, or work specifically for God can still act and hand over the results; that release, done with self-control, is a real path in its own right.

commentaries.gist: If you cannot even be intent on works for the Lord, then act while renouncing all acts in him, and give up their fruit. The next verse goes on to praise this abandonment.

For one too unready for works that ripen into love of God: take up contemplation of the self (the path of chapters 1-6), doing works without craving reward. This purifies, leads to self-vision, and finally to supreme love of God.

An alternative for one who cannot steadily perform rites for the Lord: surrender to him and give up the fruit of all acts, thinking 'I act as he directs within my ability; results are his.' Living so, grace brings blessedness.

Calls this the easiest path, the last after meditation (12.8), practice (12.9) and work for the Lord (12.10). Even acts done from personal motives can be offered to God as duty, fruits renounced, senses controlled.

practical_reading: Teachers offer it to people who feel they 'can't do spirituality properly': keep doing your ordinary work, but do it well and let go of how it lands; that release is itself the practice.
misreadings: Not 'stop caring about results' or giving up planning; it is giving up the anxious claim on outcomes.
Not a lesser or second-class path in Sridhara and Sivananda; it is presented as fully valid (Shankara does rank it lower, as a means for one who cannot follow the higher paths).
cautions: Shankara frames this as the course for someone not able to take up the higher paths; avoid presenting the reader as 'failing' the earlier rungs.
Theistic framing (taking refuge in God) may not suit every reader.
speaks_to: someone who feels too busy, scattered or tired for meditation or prayer
a person stuck on whether their work will succeed
someone who feels spiritually inadequate and needs an entry point
not_for: someone whose results genuinely matter for survival (job loss, medical outcome) and may hear 'let go of results' as 'don't try'
a reader who needs a call to agency rather than release

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 12.12 (same number in all editions checked)
translation_note: Accurate. Ramanuja reads the comparatives differently: not a ranking of value but a sequence of fallback means, each 'preferable' for someone who cannot manage the previous one; the line follows the plain reading.
context: Having offered the ladder in 12.8-11, Krishna praises its last step. Knowledge, meditation and renouncing the fruit of action are compared, ending with peace that follows at once from renunciation. Then 12.13-20 begin the portrait of the devotee who is dear to him.

key_terms.sense: giving up the fruit of action
from that giving up, peace follows immediately

core_teaching: Releasing one's claim on the results of action brings peace without delay; the commentators read the ranking as encouragement to take up this step, not as a literal claim that it outranks meditation for everyone.

commentaries.gist: Knowledge beats unenlightened practice, meditation beats knowledge, and abandoning the fruit beats meditation, ending samsara at once. But this is praise to inspire the less able, as one praises today's brahmins by recalling Agastya drinking the ocean.

If devotion is too hard, try self-knowledge; failing that, contemplation of the self; failing that, works with their fruit given up. That removes sin and brings peace, which leads back up to contemplation, self-vision and supreme love of God.

Knowledge grounded in teaching and reasoning surpasses practice without understanding; meditation surpasses that; renouncing the fruit surpasses meditation, because non-attachment plus the Lord's grace quickly brings release from worldly existence.

Follows Shankara: the ranking praises renouncing fruits to spur aspirants into selfless action. Adds that desire is the enemy of peace; renouncing fruits purifies the heart and weakens desire, and the sage does it naturally.

practical_reading: Used to say that peace is not earned only by long meditation: the moment you stop gripping the outcome of a task, the agitation around it eases.
misreadings: Not a claim that meditation and study are worthless.
Not 'stop caring how things turn out'; peace comes from releasing the grip, not from indifference.
Not a promise that circumstances improve at once; it is the mind that settles.
cautions: Shankara explicitly calls the ranking 'mere praise'; a reading should not overstate it as a literal hierarchy.
speaks_to: someone exhausted by over-investing in outcomes (exams, promotions, launches)
a person who finds sitting meditation hard and feels behind
anxiety about results
not_for: someone in acute grief, where 'peace at once' may sound glib
a person facing an outcome they cannot afford to let go of without support

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 12.14 (same in all editions checked; Shankara and Sridhara comment on 12.13-14 together)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Yogī' is glossed variously: Shankara as steadfast in thought, Ramanuja as always engaged in meditation on spirit, Sivananda as evenness of mind; 'steady in practice' is fair. The misuse field is empty in our data; suggested text below.
context: Second verse of the eight-verse portrait (12.13-20) of the devotee Krishna loves, continuing the sentence begun in 12.13 (no hatred, friendliness, compassion, no 'mine' or 'I', even in pain and pleasure, forgiving). Each verse ends with the refrain 'such a one is dear to me'.

key_terms.sense: with mind and understanding offered to me
that one is dear to me

core_teaching: The person God loves is inwardly settled: content whatever they receive, disciplined, clear about what is true, and with thinking and feeling directed to God.

commentaries.gist: With 12.13, marks of the renunciate: content whether or not bodily needs are met, steadfast in thought, firmly convinced of the Self's nature, mind and reason given to the Lord. Expands 7.17's 'the wise are dear to me'.

Applies it to the karma-yogi: content with whatever chance brings for bodily needs, always meditating on the self as distinct from matter, firm in the scriptural knowledge of spirit, convinced that works done without seeking reward are worship of Vasudeva.

Treats 13-14 as the traits that quickly win grace: contented whether or not things are gained, cheerful, vigilant, self-restrained, firm in conviction about the Lord, mind and intellect dedicated to him.

Such a person is content because they see what comes as the fruit of past actions; satisfied with little, never grumbling about food or clothing, fixed on the Absolute through steady meditation and self-surrender.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a portrait to grow toward: contentment that does not depend on getting things, steady habits, and a settled sense of what you live for.
misreadings: Contentment here is not complacency or giving up on improving one's circumstances.
Not a test the reader must already pass to be loved; it describes a direction of growth.
cautions: Sivananda grounds contentment in past karma ('what comes is the fruit of your past actions'), which can feel blaming to someone suffering.
Shankara applies the list to monastic renunciates; a lay reader should not be made to feel excluded.
speaks_to: restlessness and constant wanting more
someone building a daily discipline
a person seeking an inner anchor amid changing circumstances
not_for: someone in material hardship, who may hear 'be content' as 'accept deprivation'
a reader feeling unlovable, if framed as conditions for being dear to God
research_note: Suggested misuse text: 'Contentment is not settling for less or giving up on change; it is not being ruled by wanting.'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 12.15 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Amarṣa' is rendered variously: 'envy' (Sastri's Shankara, Sridhara's 'jealousy at another's gain'), 'wrath' (Govindacharya's Ramanuja), 'anger' (Sivananda); 'impatience/intolerance' is also standard. our_note's claim that Shankara glosses amarsha as 'intolerance' is not visible in Sastri's abridged English, which glosses only harsha (joy); it may come from the Sanskrit bhashya. our_note's 'Ramanuja takes them as feelings directed at other beings' is roughly supported: Govindacharya renders him as not being the author of joy to one or wrath to another.
context: Part of the eight-verse portrait (12.13-20) of the devotee dear to Krishna. After content and self-control (12.14), this verse turns to relationships: the person is no source of fear to others and is not shaken by them, and is free of four disturbing emotions.

key_terms.sense: from whom the world does not shrink / is not agitated
who is not agitated by the world
elation, exhilaration at getting what one wants
impatience, intolerance; also read as envy or anger

core_teaching: The person God loves threatens no one and is not threatened by anyone; free of elation, resentment, fear and agitation, they are safe to be around and hard to unsettle.

commentaries.gist: Applies it to the renunciate. Joy is the mind's exhilaration on getting what it desired, showing in bristling hair and tears; one free of joy, envy, fear and sorrow is dear to the Lord.

This person never acts so as to trouble the world, and nothing the world does can trouble him, since he has no antagonism toward anyone; so he gives rise to neither delight nor anger in others' regard.
No one feels threatened by him, nor he by anyone. Elation is joy at getting what one wants, jealousy is envy at another's gain, fear is terror, anxiety a mind ruffled by fear; he is free of all four.

The devotee harms no creature in thought, word or deed, so none fears him; seeing the world as his own Self, he fears nothing. Joy, anger, fear and anxiety leave him on their own, like animals fleeing a forest fire.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to everyday relationships: be someone people feel safe around, and do not let others' moods or opinions set your own.
misreadings: Not 'never disagree or cause any discomfort'; it means not causing needless harm or fear.
Not suppressing emotion; it describes freedom from being driven by it.
cautions: For someone being harmed by others, 'not agitated by the world' must not imply they should simply absorb mistreatment.
speaks_to: someone who is easily rattled by others' reactions
a person aware that their temper unsettles family or colleagues
workplace or family conflict
not_for: someone in an abusive situation, who may hear it as 'don't be upset by it'
acute anxiety disorder, if presented as a standard to meet rather than a direction

'Capable' for dakṣa is fine (Sridhara: not lazy; Shankara: able to decide rightly on the spot). The line's 'not chasing every new venture' is a fair modern gloss. context: Continues the portrait of the beloved devotee (12.13-20). After the social marks of 12.15, this verse lists practical and inner traits: wanting nothing extra, clean, competent, impartial, untroubled, and no longer launching desire-driven projects.

key_terms.sense: one who has given up (self-driven) undertakings

core_teaching: The beloved devotee is not dependent on things, is clean and competent, stays impartial and untroubled, and has stopped launching projects out of craving.

commentaries.gist: Indifferent to body, senses and objects; pure inside and out; able to decide rightly on the spot; not taking a friend's side; habitually giving up actions aimed at desired objects of this world or the next.

Wants nothing but the self; keeps the body on scripturally allowed food; skilled in enjoined duties; unconcerned with other matters; unmoved by the heat, cold and hardship those duties bring; drops every undertaking that scripture does not require.

Indifferent even to things that come unasked; clean within and without; dexterous, meaning not lazy; not taking sides; free of anguish; habitually giving up undertakings aimed at visible or unseen results.

Free of dependence; purity outer (washing) and inner (uprooting likes, dislikes, lust, anger); prompt and skilful; unaffected by wrongs done to him; has given up ego-driven initiative and lets the divine will act through him.

practical_reading: Teachers draw from it a picture of calm competence: do what is yours to do well and promptly, keep inner and outer life clean, and stop piling on new pursuits driven by wanting.
misreadings: 'Giving up all undertakings' is not quitting work or ambition; the commentators limit it to desire-driven ventures (Ramanuja keeps all enjoined duty).
'Unconcerned' is impartiality, not apathy.
'Pure' is not a matter of ritual status.
cautions: Sivananda's 'not troubled even if beaten by a wicked man' should not be presented as advice to endure abuse.

a person who wants to be dependable and calm at work
decision fatigue and scattered energy
not_for: someone who has lost motivation or is depressed, who might hear 'give up undertakings' as permission to withdraw
a young person just starting out who needs encouragement to begin things

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 12.17 (same in all editions checked)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Śubhāśubha-parityāgī' is read by all four commentators as giving up good and bad actions (merit and demerit), not good and bad outcomes; the line's 'letting go of good and bad outcomes' shifts the sense from actions to results. Acceptable as an application, but note it.
context: Part of the portrait of the beloved devotee (12.13-20). It restates and deepens 12.13's evenness: four reactions (exulting, hating, grieving, craving) are named and set aside, along with attachment to good and bad deeds.

key_terms.sense: one who has given up both good and bad (acts, merit and demerit)

core_teaching: The devotee is not thrown about by gain and loss: no exulting, hating, grieving or craving, and no clinging even to merit, since both good and bad works bind.

commentaries.gist: He does not rejoice on gaining the desirable, does not fret at the undesirable, does not grieve at parting with something loved, and does not long for what he lacks.

The karma-yogi neither exults at what delights people nor hates the opposite, does not grieve at losses such as wife, son or wealth, does not crave prosperity, and gives up both merit and sin, since both bind alike.
Neither pleased by the pleasant nor upset by the unpleasant, not grieving at losing what was wanted nor longing for the unattained; habitually renouncing merit and demerit, and devoted.

Expands 12.13: he does not rejoice in getting desirable things, hate the undesirable, grieve at parting from loved ones, or crave the unattained; he has renounced the good and evil actions that bring pleasure and pain.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to emotional swings: notice the cycle of thrill, resentment, grief and craving, and practise not being carried away by it, without pretending not to feel.
misreadings: Not 'feeling grief is wrong'; the ideal is not being swept away, and this is a description of a mature devotee, not a rule for the bereaved.
'Giving up good and evil' is not moral indifference; it means not clinging even to merit.
cautions: Explicitly names not grieving; Ramanuja's example is the loss of wife, son or wealth. Do not use on day 1 of a grief plan or for someone recently bereaved.
'Renouncing good and evil' can be misheard as relativism.
speaks_to: someone caught in emotional highs and lows over outcomes
a person whose mood depends on wins and losses
envy and craving
not_for: fresh grief or bereavement
someone who has been told not to show emotion and needs permission to feel

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 12.18 (same in all editions checked; grammatically one sentence with 12.19, and Shankara, Sridhara and Ramanuja comment on 12.18-19 together)
translation_note: Accurate. Ends with a comma because the sentence completes in 12.19 ('that person is dear to me'); a reading built on 12.18 alone should know the predicate is in the next verse.

key_terms.sense: the same toward enemy and friend
in cold and heat, pleasure and pain

core_teaching: Evenness across the pairs of opposites, including how one is treated by others, marks the devotee; it rests on having no attachment.

commentaries.gist: Read with 12.19 for the renunciate who knows the Supreme: he has no attachment to any object, is content with the bare means of bodily sustenance, and his thought rests steadily on the highest reality.
12.13 already ruled out hating foe or friend; here the equanimity is stronger: staying even when actually face to face with them, and bearing honour and disgrace alike.
Same to foe and friend; even in honour and dishonour, meaning free of joy and sorrow at them; alike in heat and cold, happiness and misery; not attached to anything.
The ordinary person is ruled by honour and dishonour, cold and heat, pleasure and pain; the devotee keeps a balanced mind, unmoved by attraction and repulsion, and is attached to nothing.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to criticism and praise at work and in families: your worth is not set by who flatters or insults you, and you can treat a rival with the same fairness as a friend.
misreadings: Being the same in insult does not mean tolerating abuse; it means one's worth is not decided by it.
'Same to enemy and friend' is not naivety about who is safe; it is freedom from hatred and favouritism.
cautions: Incomplete sentence: pair with 12.19 or note that it continues.
For someone being harassed or abused, 'stay even in dishonour' must not be framed as 'accept it'.

office politics and rivalry
someone whose self-worth swings with others' opinions
not_for: someone currently in an abusive relationship or facing discrimination
acute humiliation or public shaming, if offered without compassion first

key_terms.sense: one for whom blame and praise weigh the same
without a fixed home / not attached to home

core_teaching: The devotee is unmoved by praise or blame, sparing with words, content with whatever comes, not bound to a home or comfort, and steady in mind; such a person is dear to God.

commentaries.gist: Content with bare bodily needs, citing the Mahabharata's ideal of one dressed in anything, eating anything, sleeping anywhere; homeless as another smriti says; thought fixed on the Supreme. Concludes the marks of renunciates devoted to the imperishable.

'Without a home' means free of love for house and the like, the mind being set on the self; such a person bears honour and disgrace equally and is dear to the Lord. This closes the account of bhakti-yoga.
Praise and censure alike; reticent, with speech controlled; satisfied with whatever is obtained; having no fixed shelter; steady or sober in mind; such a devoted person is dear to the Lord.

Neither elated by praise nor hurt by blame; silent in speech and thought; content with the bare means of life; homeless, treating the world as his dwelling; mind ever fixed on Brahman. Cites the same Mahabharata verse as Shankara.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to approval-seeking: let praise and criticism pass through, speak less, be content with enough, and hold possessions and places lightly.
misreadings: Not 'never ask for credit' or never advocate for yourself.
'Homeless' is not a recommendation to abandon family or housing for a lay reader; even Ramanuja reads it as non-attachment to home.
'Silent' is not shutting people out.
cautions: Literal 'homeless' (Shankara, Sridhara, Sivananda) describes a wandering renunciate; it may land badly with someone facing housing insecurity.
Our line paraphrases aniketa as 'not status', which is not supported by the commentaries.

people-pleasing
a person seeking simplicity and contentment
not_for: someone who is actually homeless or displaced
a person being silenced or whose voice needs to be heard
